extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and math communicators (especially graduate students) interested in starting or improving a math blog
extracted.subtask_description: Creating expository math blog posts (often by graduate students) that distill advanced ideas into accessible, illustrated explanations and serve both as learning tools and public-facing writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as a learning tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The learning process often involved writing. I learn best by putting my thoughts on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing helps slow down and think carefully about mathematics, allowing ideas to 'simmer' into 'aha moments.' Use writing as a study skill: compose mini expositions for yourself and later polish them for the blog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distill ideas; fight through formalities and jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Quite often, I’d find that the ideas of math are hidden behind a dense fog of formalities and technical jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time distilling and rephrasing technical material to reveal the underlying ideas. Aim to make advanced mathematics accessible to a wide range of readers by removing unnecessary jargon and focusing on core concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't worry about frequency; blog when you have time
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t worry about frequency. I blog only when I have time, and I think this has worked out well so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid internal or external pressure to publish on a strict schedule. Write primarily for yourself; publish when you have something meaningful to share rather than to meet a cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hand-drawn illustrations for a personal touch
rubrics_metrics.description: The blog’s most frequently asked question is how I make the illustrations. It’s super easy! I draw them by hand with pen and paper, snap a photo with my phone, Airdrop to my computer, and edit (add color, etc.) with Photoshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand-drawn pictures are an affordable, personal option (preferred over pen tablets by the author). Practical workflow: draw on paper, photograph, transfer to computer, and lightly edit for clarity and color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and pictures to demystify concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrates through examples and pictures, how you can make new vectors from old using the direct sum and the tensor product (example: 'The Tensor Product Demystified').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage concrete examples, comparisons, and visuals to explain abstract concepts (e.g., Yoneda perspective, quantum vs classical probability). Visuals and worked examples help readers build intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose topics that bridge areas and connect to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Category Theory provides a bridge between different areas of mathematics and its objects... Similarly, Tai-Danae’s blog and its great content is a bridge between many wonderful areas of math and its readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics that highlight connections across fields and that can serve as a unifying narrative for diverse audiences. Framing material as 'bridges' can make content more broadly relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make posts a personal, public record of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Math3ma is a public record of this personal endeavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the blog as a reflective space documenting your learning process. Personal voice and anecdotes are appropriate and can make posts more engaging and authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurpose and polish personal notes into posts
rubrics_metrics.description: After my first semester I’d already amassed lots of mini expositions I’d written for myself. So I had all these little essays laying around and eventually decided to share them online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save study notes and mini-expositions; later revise and polish them for publication. This is an efficient way to generate content that is already pedagogically oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for clarity: learn to 'see' mathematics clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: I wanted to go to graduate school—to learn how to see mathematics clearly. The articles on Math3ma are my personal attempts at fighting through the fog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity of presentation and conceptual understanding over formal completeness. Spend the effort to uncover and present the simple ideas underlying technical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical production workflow tip
rubrics_metrics.description: I draw them by hand with pen and paper, snap a photo with my phone, Airdrop to my computer, and edit (add color, etc.) with Photoshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minimal, low-cost workflow for producing illustrations: pen-and-paper drawing → photograph → transfer to computer → light digital editing. Emphasizes accessibility and low barrier to entry.
